Lessons.Title: How Would You Describe These Figures?
ExplanationParagraphs: Grade 4, Unit 7 Lesson 1 (IM First Edition 2021): students describe and copy geometric figures, using increasingly precise everyday language about points, lines and parts of lines. The aim is not yet to demand formal definitions of lines versus segments; the next lesson introduces these terms more formally.

Original teacher sequence: Notice and Wonder about string art (5 minutes), back-to-back Do You See What I See? pairs with four blackline-master image cards (25 minutes), draw five long straight lines on an isometric dot field and trace familiar figures (15 minutes), synthesis (10 minutes), Lines and More Cool-down (5 minutes).

Warm-up: display original string-art source or a teacher-chosen first-party line arrangement. Invite students to name and locate points, straight strokes, intersections and directions. Informal terms are welcome; ask how language could be more precise for a drawing partner.

For the back-to-back activity, two partners take turns describing a figure without showing it; the listener draws using a straightedge. Use two rounds then switch roles for two more. Compare the original and redraw, identify what details are missing, and revise words for position, orientation, starting points and endpoints. The four publisher blackline cards are not reproduced here; a teacher may make independent equivalent cards.

Dot field: draw exactly five extended straight lines, each connecting two or more dots; mark one shape/letter built from portions of those lines and discuss how those shorter pieces begin and end. Show examples of parts of lines without demanding a premature technical distinction in this first geometry lesson.

First-party Edulytics Cool-down: privately describe a simple two-line figure to a partner, who redraws and marks two clearly described points. The teacher compares how successfully the words communicate location and orientation. This is an open drawing/oral assessment, not a publisher-supplied or machine-scored item.

KeyConcepts.Title: Geometric points as locations
KeyConcepts.Definition: A dot or a crossing marks a location that can be named when describing an image.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Specify the position of a point relative to other marks rather than pointing vaguely.
KeyConcepts.Example: Say 'The top point is directly above the centre of the bottom edge' instead of 'Put it here'.

KeyConcepts.Title: Directional language for straight marks
KeyConcepts.Definition: Describe where a straight stroke goes, which points it passes through, and whether it continues toward the edge.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use horizontal, vertical, crossing, extends, left/right, top/bottom and meaningful relative positions.
KeyConcepts.Example: Draw a straight horizontal stroke passing through two dots in the middle row; extend it toward both edges.

KeyConcepts.Title: Short portions of longer straight lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: Figures can use a portion of a larger straight line with visible start and stop locations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare the full straight stroke with the shorter part that forms an edge; formal terminology comes next lesson.
KeyConcepts.Example: The side of a triangle is a shorter part of one of the long straight strokes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up: describe string art without guessing counts
WorkedExamples.Question: Look at the teacher-provided original string-art image or an independently drawn web of intersecting straight strokes. What do you notice and wonder?
Steps: Name a visible type of mark: straight strokes, intersections or coloured lines.
Describe where two marks cross or where several marks point without relying on the words 'there' or 'here'.
Listen to a classmate's observation and make its positional wording more precise.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Open observations and questions; teacher judges geometric vocabulary and reference to the actual image.
WorkedExamples.Check: No machine-scored count or publisher-image inference.

WorkedExamples.Title: Back-to-back figure reconstruction (teacher-led)
WorkedExamples.Question: Partner A sees a figure card and describes it without showing it. Partner B draws only from the description. How can they make a closer match?
WorkedExamples.Method: Oral instructions and partner drawing, not scalar Practice.
Steps: Tell B where to place the first visible point and identify a direction for the first straight stroke.
Specify how later strokes meet or cross and whether they continue or stop at a particular point.
Compare the card with B's sketch; identify a misunderstood length, location or direction and try a more precise description.
Switch roles and repeat using the other two cards.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A corresponding drawing plus revised descriptions; the teacher compares the two images.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original publisher four-card blackline master not copied; teacher provides or independently constructs equivalent cards.

WorkedExamples.Title: Five lines through dots
WorkedExamples.Question: On a teacher-provided isometric dot field, draw five long straight lines, each passing through at least two dots. Highlight one familiar shape or letter made from portions of those lines.
Steps: Use a straightedge to draw a first line passing through at least two separate dots.
Make four additional extended lines with the same minimum-two-dot condition.
Trace a triangle, quadrilateral or letter formed by selected shorter parts of the lines.
Explain which crossings or dots identify start and stop locations along the traced figure.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Five qualifying lines and a highlighted figure; the teacher checks straightness, dots, and explanations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Five separate qualifying long lines, not five counted finite isolated segments.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent Edulytics Cool-down: describe for a redraw
WorkedExamples.Question: Describe to a partner a drawing containing one horizontal and one vertical straight stroke crossing at a point, and two additional marked dots on the horizontal stroke. The partner must redraw it from your words.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party communication-and-drawing rubric; not publisher Cool-down.
Steps: State the direction of the first stroke and its location on the page.
Describe where the second stroke crosses the first and where the two dots sit relative to that crossing.
The partner redraws and points out the crossing and two marked dots.
Compare both versions and correct one imprecise phrase, if needed.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Teacher-reviewed redraw showing one crossing and two distinct marked points with clear spatial descriptions.
WorkedExamples.Check: Open-ended task; do not infer success from a numeric or multiple-choice response.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Describing a figure only as 'a big triangle over there'.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Its position, orientation, and intersections remain ambiguous for the drawing partner.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Give two or more landmarks and directions, then compare the redraw to the target.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling every short stroke or edge a whole extended line and requiring formal definitions too early.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The first lesson builds intuitive recognition and language, with formal distinctions in the next lesson.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Discuss longer strokes and their shorter portions in ordinary precise words; accept informal language that accurately describes a figure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Drawing five isolated strokes that connect fewer than two dots each.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source task explicitly requires five long straight lines through at least two dots apiece.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check and revise each drawn line against the two-dot and straightedge conditions.

SummaryPoints: Use points, locations and directional words to communicate a geometric image precisely.
The original back-to-back activity includes four cards, two drawings per partner; teacher compares descriptions and sketches.
Five long lines must each connect at least two dots; shorter traced portions can form shapes or letters.
The 2021 lesson introduces geometric language intuitively and does not require formal line/segment definitions yet.
The independent Cool-down and partner drawing require teacher review; there is no machine-scored scalar Practice analogue.

Visuals.Title: Teacher's first-party vocabulary card
Visuals.Description: Text landmarks and spatial descriptions for independently drawn cards, not publisher blackline artwork.
Visuals.PrimaryLabel: Point A, horizontal stroke, point B
Items: Point A lies above point B.
A straight horizontal stroke extends left and right through B.
A second vertical stroke crosses it at B.
SecondaryItems: Teacher checks the actual reproduced positions with a drawing.

Visuals.Title: Dot-field construction checklist
Visuals.Description: Text instructions accompany a real isometric dot field supplied by teacher.
Visuals.SecondaryLabel: Each passes through at least two dots
Items: 1. Each of five strokes is straight.
2. Each crosses two or more dots.
3. Highlight a shorter part that forms a familiar shape.
SecondaryItems: Original dots and hand drawing are not supplied as a falsely certified digital image.

Visuals.Title: Back-to-back partner communication
Visuals.Description: Independently authored process guidance, not publisher visual asset.
Items: Partner A describes points and directions.
Partner B draws using a straightedge without seeing the card.
Compare the drawings and revise ambiguous wording.
SecondaryItems: Teacher reviews all four real image cards and student drawings.
